label: Real Projective Spaces and Projective Shape
notes: Spanning printed pages 147 through 155, this chapter moves nonparametric inference from spheres to real projective space, the natural home for axial data and for shape under perspective imaging. We motivate why antipodal identification and projective invariance force a quotient sample space rather than ordinary Euclidean coordinates.

label: Lines Through the Origin
notes: Real projective space collects one-dimensional subspaces of Euclidean space, so a datum is a direction without a chosen sign or scale. We stress that any nonzero representative names the same projective point, which is exactly why axial measurements like crystal orientations belong here naturally.

label: The Antipodal Quotient
notes: Identifying each unit vector with its negative collapses the sphere into real projective space, a smooth compact manifold of the same dimension. The double cover viewpoint explains why local charts work yet no global sign convention exists, which the notebook visual makes concrete on the two-sphere.

label: Projective Distance
notes: Because antipodes coincide, the natural distance compares unsigned directions through the acute angle between representative lines. We show the chordal surrogate built from the outer product, motivating the embedding of the next slide and explaining why naive spherical distance double counts antipodal pairs.

label: The Veronese Embedding
notes: Mapping a unit representative to its outer product sends real projective space equivariantly into symmetric matrices, erasing sign because the outer product of a vector and its negative agree. This embedding is the workhorse that converts intrinsic projective questions into ordinary linear algebra on matrices.

label: Extrinsic Mean as Leading Eigenvector
notes: The extrinsic mean is found by averaging the embedded outer products and projecting back, which Rayleigh's principle identifies with the top eigenvector of the average matrix. Existence and uniqueness reduce to a simple spectral gap condition between the first and second eigenvalues.

label: CLT and Two-Sample Tests
notes: A central limit theorem in the tangent space of the embedded mean yields asymptotic normality, supporting bootstrap confidence regions and chi-squared style two-sample tests. We emphasize that all inference happens after the equivariant embedding, where Euclidean asymptotics legitimately apply.

label: Pinhole Imaging and Projective Transforms
notes: A pinhole camera maps a scene to the image plane up to an unknown projective transformation, so two photographs of one rigid scene differ by a homography. This is why recognition must factor out the whole projective group rather than only similarity transformations as in Kendall shape.

label: Projective Invariants: the Cross-Ratio
notes: The cross-ratio of four collinear points is the fundamental projective invariant, unchanged by any perspective map. We compute it explicitly and note that such invariants, or a registered projective frame, are what let us define a shape that survives arbitrary camera viewpoints.

label: Projective Shape Space
notes: Fixing a projective frame on a configuration registers the remaining points into projective coordinates, so a projective shape becomes a point in a product of real projective spaces. This product manifold inherits extrinsic means, embeddings, and the limit theory developed earlier in the chapter.

label: Application: Invariant Scene Recognition
notes: Combining the embedding, the extrinsic mean, and the projective-frame shape gives a pipeline that recognizes scenes invariantly under perspective. The notebook lab asks students to break invariance deliberately and watch the statistic change, proving the geometry is load bearing rather than decorative.

label: Recap and Bridge
notes: We close by tracing the route from sample space to inference: lines through the origin, antipodal quotient, Veronese embedding, eigenvector mean, and the projective frame. This scaffolding carries directly into later chapters that apply the same extrinsic machinery to richer shape spaces.
